beats.beat: Lodging at the Bell on credit he can ill afford, Farr seeks out Judith Vane, who knew him before he went to war.
Judith takes him to her brother Owen's shop, where Owen is reluctant to be drawn into a quarrel with gentry.
Owen consults his dispensing book and finds the entry for the very date the will was signed.
The entry shows Fenner was given a heavy dose against pain that same morning, and Owen recalls the old man could scarcely say his own name that day.
Judith concludes that a dispensing book alone will not answer, and that they need someone who was inside Oakmere on the day of the signing.

turn.note: Judith's decision to go to Oakmere under pretence of parish alms sets up the next chapter's action directly.

problems: "which is a kind of charity that costs a man more than it saves him" is a narratorial aphorism disconnected from any character's specific voice.
"He is exact with dates and numbers, and he cannot bear to be asked a thing he can answer and leave it unanswered" tells the reader a trait the following dialogue already demonstrates.
